summary: An island country in the eastern Mediterranean, once ruled by the Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Venetians, Ottomans and British; since 1974 the north has been controlled by Turkish Cypriots and the island has remained divided.

ranking.name: Greek Orthodoxy (Church of Cyprus)
ranking.description: According to tradition, the apostle Paul and Barnabas, a native of Cyprus, came to the island to preach in AD 45, which makes the Church of Cyprus one of the oldest Christian churches; the Council of Ephesus in 431 recognized its autocephalous status. After the Ottoman conquest of 1571, the “millet system,” which distinguished communities by religion, made the archbishop the political leader of the Greek population, and at independence in 1960 Archbishop Makarios III even became the first president. Orthodoxy has thus been closely bound up with Greek Cypriot national identity, and the proportion of believers is extremely high.

ranking.name: Other Christian (Catholic, Protestant, Armenian Church, Maronite)
ranking.description: Armenians have been on the island since the Byzantine era, and another group of refugees arrived after the Armenian genocide of 1915; Maronites migrated from Lebanon roughly between the 8th and 12th centuries; Catholicism (Latin rite) can be traced to the Lusignan dynasty (1192–1489) and later Venetian rule, while British colonial rule (1878–1960) brought Anglicanism. In recent years foreign workers from the Philippines and elsewhere have also increased the number of Catholics.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: After the Ottoman conquest of 1571, Turkish settlers and some converted residents formed the Turkish Cypriots, who follow Sunni Islam and make up nearly two-tenths of the island’s population. After Turkey’s military intervention in 1974 and the division of the island, most Turkish Cypriots concentrated in the north, so in the south, which is actually administered by the Republic of Cyprus, Muslims are only a minority, mainly Turkish Cypriot residents and immigrants from the Middle East and South Asia.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Because Orthodoxy has long been tied to national identity and national holidays, the proportion of people declaring no religion is very low. In recent years, with urbanization, study abroad and Europeanization (accession to the EU in 2004), the number of young people who rarely go to church has gradually grown, but most still take part in religious rites on occasions such as baptisms, weddings and Easter.

religion.background: Cyprus accepted Christianity in the apostolic age, and Byzantine rule planted Orthodoxy deep in people’s hearts. After the Crusader era beginning in 1191, the Frankish Lusignan dynasty and the Venetians brought Catholicism and suppressed Orthodoxy; the Ottoman conquest of 1571 instead restored the standing of the Orthodox Church while introducing Islam. During British colonial rule, the Orthodox Church led the movement for union with Greece. After the division of 1974, the south is predominantly Greek Orthodox and the north predominantly Muslim, and religious and ethnic boundaries largely coincide.

language.official: The official languages are Greek and Turkish.

ranking.name: Greek (Cypriot dialect)
ranking.description: Around the 12th–11th centuries BC, Mycenaean Greeks settled in Cyprus and brought the Greek language, and in antiquity the island even developed its own Cypriot syllabary. Through Byzantine, Frankish, Venetian and Ottoman rule, the local spoken language developed into the Cypriot dialect, which preserves many archaic sounds and foreign words, while standard Modern Greek is used in formal settings and schools. Greek Cypriots make up the great majority of the population in the south, so Greek is the principal language.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: After the Ottoman conquest of 1571, Turkish settlers settled on the island, forming a Turkish-speaking Turkish Cypriot community. The 1960 constitution made Turkish an official language alongside Greek; after the division of 1974 almost all Turkish Cypriots moved to the north, and the north also received immigrants from mainland Turkey, so Turkish is used mainly in Northern Cyprus.

ranking.name: Russian and other languages
ranking.description: After the Soviet Union collapsed in the 1990s, large numbers of Russians and Ukrainians moved to places such as Limassol, running shipping, finance and real estate businesses, and Limassol was at one time jokingly called “Limassolgrad”; after the Russia–Ukraine war of 2022 a new wave of immigrants arrived. Together with Bulgarian and Romanian workers after EU accession in 2004, and domestic helpers from the Philippines and Sri Lanka, they form a diverse set of minority-language groups.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: In 1878 Britain obtained administration of Cyprus from the Ottoman Empire, made it a Crown colony in 1925, and held it until independence in 1960. English was therefore long the language of administration, law and higher education, and is still widely used today in business, tourism and on road signs; the British Sovereign Base Areas on the island and large numbers of British retirees also mean that quite a few people have English as their mother tongue.

language.history: After the Greeks arrived in Cyprus in the Late Bronze Age, Greek became the main language of the island and was once written in a distinctive syllabary. Greek held a secure position in the Byzantine period; Frankish and Venetian rule brought French and Italian loanwords, and Ottoman rule after 1571 introduced Turkish. During British colonial rule (1878–1960) English became the administrative language. After the division of 1974, the areas where Greek and Turkish are used have been roughly split between south and north, while recent waves of immigration have made Russian and other languages increasingly common in the cities.

ranking.name: Halloumi cheese
ranking.description: A semi-hard brined cheese made from goat’s and sheep’s milk, with a high melting point; when grilled or fried it turns golden outside and springy inside, with a slightly salty, chewy texture.
ranking.history: Halloumi has been made in Cyprus for hundreds of years and is recorded in documents from the Venetian period in the 16th century. In the past herders needed a cheese that could be kept for a long time in the hot climate, so they cooked the curds and then soaked them in brine, adding mint leaves for aroma. It is a traditional food shared by Greek and Turkish Cypriots (called hellim in Turkish), received EU Protected Designation of Origin status in 2021, and is also an important export of the country.

ranking.name: Souvlaki
ranking.description: Marinated pork or chicken is cut into chunks, skewered and grilled over charcoal, tucked into a large pita, and eaten with tomato, cucumber, onion and parsley.
ranking.history: The practice of grilling meat on skewers can be traced to ancient Greece, where the Homeric epics describe roasting sacrificial meat on spits. Cypriot souvlakia are bigger chunks than those in mainland Greece and are often grilled on the traditional rectangular charcoal grill known as a “foukou.” Family barbecues outdoors on Sundays or holidays are an important social activity there, and gatherings after Easter often feature it as the star.

ranking.name: Kleftiko
ranking.description: Bone-in lamb is sealed together with potatoes, bay leaves and lemon and slow-roasted for several hours in a traditional clay oven until the meat is so tender it falls off the bone.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Greek “kleftis” (thief), alluding to the Greek “klepht” guerrillas of the Ottoman period, who stole sheep and buried them in sealed earth pits to cook slowly so that the smoke would not give away their hiding place. Many Cypriot households have a domed clay oven, the “fourni,” in the yard, used on weekends or religious holidays to cook this dish. It symbolizes the popular memory of resistance to foreign rule and is also a signature dish of village feasts.

ranking.name: Sheftalia
ranking.description: Minced pork mixed with onion and parsley is wrapped in caul fat into small sausages and grilled over charcoal, the fat melting into the meat and filling the air with aroma.
ranking.history: Sheftalia is a grilled dish unique to Cyprus; the name is generally thought to be related to Turkish, reflecting culinary exchange during the Ottoman period, and Turkish Cypriots have a similar “şeftali kebabı.” Wrapping meat in caul fat is a rural, frugal way of using every part of the pig. It often appears together with souvlaki at grill stalls and in the meze spreads of taverns and is an everyday favorite of the locals.

ranking.name: Meze
ranking.description: A meal made up of twenty or thirty small dishes served in succession, from olives, yogurt dips and salads to grilled meat and seafood, in portions large enough to be a whole meal.
ranking.history: The word “meze” comes from Persian, meaning “taste,” and spread across the eastern Mediterranean through Ottoman Turkish. During the three centuries of Ottoman rule in Cyprus, the habit of eating small dishes with wine became deeply rooted in local tavern culture. Cypriot meze is famous for its astonishing quantity and is often divided into meat and seafood versions; relatives and friends sit around the table and eat slowly for several hours, which is the typical way of dining at weddings, name-day celebrations and weekend gatherings.
